title: When feelings do not match the facts
description: Someone can know a thing is safe, fine, or forgiven — and still feel otherwise. Both can be true.

body.heading: Facts do not dissolve feelings
paragraphs: “But the exam is only worth ten percent” is true, and the fear remains. Feelings are not conclusions; they are weather. Arguing with weather has never once changed it, but standing in it with someone helps it pass.
This is why “There’s nothing to worry about” so rarely comforts. It answers a question the person was not asking.

body.heading: Validate, then inform
paragraphs: The order matters. First the feeling gets acknowledged: “It makes sense you’re scared; this matters to you.” Then, if facts are welcome, they can be offered — gently, and once. Reversing the order makes the facts sound like a rebuttal.
Sometimes the facts are not welcome yet, and that is fine. Information keeps. Company is what is needed now.

body.heading: Your own weather counts too
paragraphs: This works inward as well. You can know the plane is safe and still grip the armrest; know the apology was accepted and still feel ashamed. Treating your own mismatched feelings with patience, instead of contempt, is the same skill turned homeward.
Feelings catch up to facts eventually, at walking pace. Your job — with others and yourself — is to walk alongside, not to drag.

takeaway: Acknowledge the feeling first; offer facts second, gently, and only if they are welcome.
